title: Asian Games Gold Medallist Ritu Negi Excluded From Rs 1 Crore Award List
excerpt: Himachal Pradesh raised its cash award for three of its Asian Games kabaddi gold medallists to Rs 1 crore each plus government jobs — leaving out Ritu Negi, the fourth member of the winning squad.
body:
• Asian Games gold medallist Ritu Negi has been left out of Himachal Pradesh's enhanced Rs 1 crore cash-award list for the women's kabaddi squad, even though she was one of four Himachali players originally named for Rs 33.33 lakh each.
  • Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu raised the award to Rs 1 crore each for Pushpa Rana, Jyoti Thakur and Bhawna Thakur after the three met him in Shimla on Monday, along with government employment in the police or sports department.
  • Team captain Pushpa Rana said the players were "very disappointed" with the original Rs 33 lakh award, and that the chief minister listened to them politely and promised the higher amount at an official function.
  • Renuka Thakur, the fast bowler in India's gold-winning women's cricket team, will also receive Rs 1 crore from the state.

Asian Games gold medallist Ritu Negi has been dropped from Himachal Pradesh's Rs 1-crore cash-award list for its kabaddi champions. The chief minister on Monday raised the award from Rs 33.33 lakh to Rs 1 crore per player for three of the four Himachali members of India's gold-winning women's kabaddi team at Aichi-Nagoya — and Negi, from Shillai in Sirmaur, is the one name missing.

India's women's kabaddi team, led by captain Pushpa Rana, defended its Asian Games title at Aichi-Nagoya, going unbeaten before beating Iran 37-34 in the final. Four of the 12-member squad were Himachali: Rana, Negi, Jyoti Thakur and Bhavna Thakur.

From Rs 33 lakh to Rs 1 crore

The dispute began on September 30, when Chief Minister Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu announced nearly Rs 5.33 crore in awards for the state's Asian Games medal winners. Under the Himachal Pradesh Sports Council Cash Award Rules, 2024, the four kabaddi gold medallists were to share about Rs 1.33 crore — Rs 33.33 lakh each.

The players went public with their displeasure. "Look, we were very disappointed because according to the sports policy, we were not being given the amount that was due to us," India captain Pushpa Rana told IANS, adding the Rs 33 lakh figure had surfaced on social media before any official word. On Monday the three met Sukhu in Shimla, were honoured with traditional Himachali caps and shawls, and walked out with the promise of Rs 1 crore each plus government employment.

"Now, after meeting him, we received a very positive response from the Chief Minister. Considering how politely he handled us and listened to us attentively, I am hopeful that the Rs 1 crore announced or promised to us will definitely be given."

— Pushpa Rana, India women's kabaddi captain

The missing name

What remains unexplained is why the enhanced award covers three players and not four. Negi was one of the four named in the September 30 announcement and was also part of the gold-winning squad in Hangzhou in 2023. No official reason has been given for her exclusion. The omission is made more awkward by the state's own messaging: sports minister Harshwardhan Chauhan listed the three who attended the meeting — while in the same statement acknowledging Negi as one of the four who "led India to the gold medal."

The three were also promised government employment — a police department post or a Youth Services and Sports Department position so they can continue competing. It is unclear whether Negi is included.

Impact and analysis

The episode captures a recurring tension in Indian sports policy: states compete to be seen as generous patrons of champions, but the generosity is negotiated case by case. Himachal's award went from one of the leaner packages to one of the stronger ones in a single meeting — after public lobbying by the players.

For women's kabaddi, the stakes are structural. It is not a sport with a professional league or endorsement market; for most players, a state reward and a government job are the material returns on an Asian Games gold. When one member of a gold-winning quartet is cut from the enhanced award without explanation, it undercuts the message the felicitation ceremony is meant to send — that the state backs its champions equally.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora, the dispute is a window into how seriously Indian states now take women's sport — and how far the machinery still has to go. Himachali communities abroad celebrated a four-woman contribution to India's gold; they will notice the uneven recognition. The broader lesson travels well: fair, rules-based reward systems beat ad hoc generosity decided in meetings.

What's next

A formal felicitation ceremony is to be organised where the Rs 1 crore awards will be presented. The question hanging over it: whether Negi's case is revisited — through a correction or at least an explanation.
